name: 300,000 RMB parcel-sorting robot
description: An industrial robot-arm sorting cell that commits to a vacuum-suction end-effector, a single robot arm, a single vision system, and a conveyor-based induction. Targets approximately 300,000 RMB total system cost for logistics parcel sorting. Per ADR-0004, alternative architectures (e.g. a mechanical-gripper end-effector) live as sibling Product nodes under the affordable_small_warehouse_automation capability rather than as intra-product routes.

targetContext.targetCost: Approximately the entry-level total system cost target (see total_system_cost metric for the authoritative value)
targetContext.targetScale: single logistics sorting cell or small line segment
targetContext.targetPerformance: commercially useful parcel throughput with low jam and intervention rates
targetContext.targetEnvironment: conveyor-based parcel flow with variable labels, packaging, sizes, and weights

name: Vision / barcode / label recognition
description: Camera, lighting, barcode scanning, OCR, and label localization capability for identifying parcels and destinations.
notes: Hard-to-develop (per ADR-0005): CV-based label localization and OCR must work under reflective/wrinkled labels, parcel deformation, glare, occlusion, and high-speed conveyor motion. Off-the-shelf barcode readers handle clean labels; the hard part is the long tail where vision degrades.

name: Industrial area-scan camera
description: Industrial camera used to capture parcel images for label reading, barcode recognition, and visual inspection under conveyor motion.
notes: Expansion frontier: next layer may include sensor size, shutter type, frame rate, interface, trigger timing, enclosure, and cost constraints.

name: Machine vision lens and optics
description: Lens and optical configuration that focus the parcel field of view onto the camera sensor with sufficient sharpness and depth of field.
notes: Expansion frontier: next layer may include focal length, working distance, field of view, aperture, filter, focus lock, and vibration sensitivity.

name: Controlled machine-vision lighting
description: Lighting hardware and control strategy that make labels, barcodes, and parcel edges visible and repeatable despite ambient variation.
notes: Expansion frontier: next layer may include ring/bar/back/dome lighting, strobe timing, glare control, wavelength, diffuser, and dust/heat constraints.

name: Vision processing compute
description: Industrial PC, smart camera, embedded processor, or accelerator that runs barcode/OCR, detection, tracking, and integration logic.
notes: Expansion frontier: next layer may include CPU/GPU/NPU choice, latency, thermal design, software stack, camera SDK, and cost.

name: Low-cost real-time vision compute integration
description: Integration method for choosing low-cost edge compute, camera SDKs, inference runtime, thermal envelope, and latency budget so parcel detection and tracking run reliably in the sorting cell.
notes: Consistency backfill: vision compute was less mature than its semiconductor supply-chain child, so this node captures the missing integration bottleneck: real-time inference, SDK coupling, latency, thermal design, and cost in the parcel-sorting cell.

name: Barcode / OCR reading software
description: Software pipeline for reading barcodes, labels, and OCR fields from parcel images and outputting a parcel identity or destination token.
notes: Expanded on 2026-06-07 into label localization, barcode decoding runtime, OCR runtime, no-read recovery, training data, and benchmark metrics. Supplier links remain candidate product-line evidence, not confirmed target-cell BOM.

name: Parcel label localization
description: Vision software that finds barcode and text label regions on parcels before decoding or OCR, including multi-label, skew, glare, and partial-occlusion cases.
notes: Localization is separated because reflective, wrinkled, and partially covered parcel labels can fail before any decoder or OCR model runs.

name: Industrial barcode decoding runtime
description: Industrial decoder runtime for 1D and 2D parcel barcodes, including high-speed conveyor operation, multiple symbologies, damaged-code handling, and reader diagnostics.
notes: The decoder layer is commercially mature in product-line evidence, but parcel-cell fit still depends on optics, lighting, speed, code quality, and integration.

name: Parcel OCR model runtime
description: OCR runtime for parcel label text such as printed addresses, route codes, service labels, or fallback tokens when barcode reads are unavailable.
notes: OCR is kept separate from barcode decoding because label text fallback has different data, latency, accuracy, and exception-handling risks.

name: Barcode / OCR no-read recovery
description: Exception-handling loop for failed barcode or OCR reads, including retry logic, confidence thresholds, diagnostics, manual keying handoff, and WCS exception routing.
notes: No-read recovery is modeled as a bottleneck because failed reads can turn an automated cell into a manual exception workflow even when readers and OCR tools are available.

name: Parcel label training dataset
description: Curated parcel-label image and annotation set for localization, OCR, no-read analysis, glare/occlusion cases, and parcel-type coverage.
notes: Dataset scope remains a frontier: the next layer should split collection, labeling, synthetic augmentation, privacy handling, and benchmark holdout coverage.

name: Barcode / OCR benchmark protocol
description: Benchmark protocol for read rate, no-read rate, false read rate, latency, damaged-label coverage, OCR confidence, and manual-exception rate under parcel-cell conditions.
notes: Benchmarking is modeled explicitly so gate reports can expose missing read-rate and exception-rate evidence instead of relying on vendor product claims.

name: Parcel detection and tracking
description: Detects parcel position, velocity, orientation, and identity as parcels move through the sorting cell.
notes: Bottleneck theme: low_jam_rate_under_parcel_variability. Hard-to-develop (per ADR-0005): real-time pose estimation of variable parcels (size, packaging, deformation, stacking, occlusion) under conveyor motion is at the frontier of CV-based object recognition. Failure mode is qualitative — robust tracking enables pick reliability; weak tracking collapses throughput.

name: Parcel pick-and-place execution subsystem
description: The execution subsystem that physically picks, pushes, or places parcels into the selected output lane or bin. It owns the robot arm body, end effector, and motion-planning dependencies instead of duplicating those dependencies at the product root.

name: Industrial robot arm body
description: The robot body for the sorting cell, including joints, links, actuators, reducers, servo drives, controller interfaces, cabling, and mounting structure.

name: Vacuum suction end-effector module
description: The parcel-contacting vacuum-suction end effector for the active v0 product, including suction cups, vacuum generation, valves, pressure sensing, and release control for variable parcel packaging.
notes: Expansion frontier: next layer should separate suction cup geometry, vacuum generator or ejector choice, compliance, vacuum sensing, materials, wear parts, dust tolerance, and parcel-contact reliability constraints. Mechanical grippers are modeled as a separate sibling Product boundary, not as an alternate route of this active suction product.

name: Vacuum suction cup array
description: Array of suction cups used to contact parcel surfaces, with selectable cup patterns for different parcel sizes and positions.
notes: Expansion frontier: next layer may include cup diameter, material, lip geometry, wear, parcel surface compatibility, and replacement cost.

name: Parcel suction-cup contact qualification
description: Qualification method for cup geometry, lip compliance, wear, leakage, replacement interval, and parcel-surface compatibility across bags, cartons, labels, tape, and deformed packaging.
notes: Consistency backfill: the cup array was less mature than its elastomer feedstock child, so this node captures the missing parcel-contact bottleneck. Mature elastomer supply does not prove robust pickup on variable logistics packaging.

name: Vacuum generator or ejector
description: Vacuum source, often a venturi/ejector or pump, that creates suction for parcel pickup through the end effector.
notes: Expansion frontier: next layer may include compressed-air consumption, flow rate, vacuum level, noise, filters, and energy cost.

name: Vacuum valves and blow-off control
description: Valves and blow-off controls used to turn suction on/off and release parcels quickly and predictably.
notes: Expansion frontier: next layer may include valve response time, per-cup control, leakage, contamination, and timing with robot motion.

name: Vacuum blow-off timing and contamination control
description: Control method for per-zone suction timing, valve response, blow-off release, leakage tolerance, dust contamination, and synchronization with robot motion.
notes: Consistency backfill: valve and blow-off control was less mature than its material child, so this node captures the missing dynamic-control bottleneck. The hard part is synchronized pickup/release behavior, not elastomer availability.

name: Vacuum pressure sensing
description: Pressure or vacuum sensing used to detect whether enough suction cups have sealed correctly to a parcel before transport.
notes: Expansion frontier: next layer may include pressure thresholds, false positives, leak detection, response time, and failure recovery.

name: Vacuum EOAT TCP and cup-array calibration
description: Calibration of suction cup positions and tool-center-point patterns so the robot can choose cup combinations and motion paths.
notes: Expansion frontier: needs better evidence for calibration workflow, tolerance, operator time, and impact on parcel pickup success.

name: Servo drive / controller
description: Servo drive electronics and control loops that command robot joint motion under timing, accuracy, and cost constraints.
notes: Expansion frontier: next layer should cover power electronics, encoder feedback, control firmware, thermal management, safety functions, and cost/reliability constraints.

name: Servo drive power stage
description: Power electronics stage that converts DC bus power into controlled motor phase currents for each robot joint servo motor.
notes: Expansion frontier: next layer may include rectifier/DC bus, inverter devices, gate drivers, protection, EMC filtering, and heat sinking.

name: Servo drive current sensing
description: Current sensing and feedback path used by the servo drive to regulate torque and detect overload or fault conditions.
notes: Expansion frontier: next layer may include shunt or Hall sensing, ADC, isolation, bandwidth, calibration, and fault thresholds.

name: Servo drive motion-control loop
description: Servo control firmware and tuning that close current, velocity, and position loops for robot joint motion.
notes: Expansion frontier: next layer may include loop rates, encoder protocols, tuning parameters, torque limits, vibration suppression, and robot payload changes.

name: Servo drive Safe Torque Off
description: Safety-rated stop function in the servo drive that removes torque-producing output without fully powering down the control electronics.
notes: Expansion frontier: next layer may include safety inputs, diagnostics, SIL/PL claims, restart behavior, and safety PLC integration.

name: Servo drive thermal and EMC design
description: Thermal management, enclosure layout, grounding, shielding, and EMC design needed for reliable multi-axis robot servo operation.
notes: Expansion frontier: needs better evidence for low-cost multi-axis cabinet layout, cooling margin, conducted emissions, and field failure modes.

name: Precision reducer / gearbox
description: Joint reducers or gearboxes that provide torque multiplication, positional repeatability, durability, and acceptable cost for the robot arm.
notes: Expansion frontier: next layer should cover reducer type, precision gears, bearings, lubrication, heat treatment, precision machining, inspection equipment, backlash, life, and supplier constraints.

name: Strain-wave reducer wave generator
description: Elliptical wave-generator assembly that deforms the flexspline and drives the meshing action in a strain-wave reducer.
notes: Expansion frontier: next layer may include elliptical hub, wave generator bearing, preload, assembly position, and fatigue constraints.

name: Strain-wave reducer flexspline
description: Thin flexible externally toothed spline that elastically deforms and meshes with the circular spline to transmit reducer output. Hard-to-develop (per ADR-0005): manufacturing process with low yield and high tolerances — thin-wall steel parts must achieve precision tooth geometry while surviving cyclic elastic deformation. Long-standing supplier concentration in Japan reflects the difficulty of matching fatigue life at low cost.
notes: Expansion frontier: next layer may include tooth machining, thin-wall forming, heat treatment, fatigue life, crack risk, and inspection. Hard-to-develop rationale: thin-wall fatigue-life tooth manufacturing is the bottleneck behind robot reducer cost; replicating Japanese-supplier quality at low cost remains a real R&D pipeline.

name: Strain-wave reducer circular spline
description: Rigid internally toothed circular spline that meshes with the flexspline and defines the gear ratio in a strain-wave reducer.
notes: Expansion frontier: next layer may include internal tooth accuracy, material, heat treatment, concentricity, and assembly tolerance.

name: Reducer output bearing
description: High-capacity output bearing, such as cross-roller or four-point bearing, that supports robot joint loads and tilting moments.
notes: Expansion frontier: next layer may include bearing type, preload, sealing, lubrication, moment load, runout, and lifetime.

name: Reducer lubrication and life testing
description: Lubrication, endurance testing, backlash verification, and life testing needed to qualify a precision robot joint reducer. Hard-to-develop (per ADR-0005): qualifying low-cost reducers for industrial duty-cycle life requires long-running endurance test fixtures, statistically valid sample sizes, and tight backlash-growth criteria — a manufacturing-process capability with low yield and slow feedback that distinguishes incumbents from new domestic suppliers.
notes: Expansion frontier: needs better evidence for actual reducer factory process, grease interval, overload failure, backlash growth, and cost. Hard-to-develop rationale: long-cycle endurance testing capability is itself a barrier — without it, low-cost reducers cannot be qualified for industrial duty cycles.

name: Industrial servo motor
description: Servo motors sized for the arm payload, speed, duty cycle, and total cost target.
notes: Expansion frontier: industrial servo motors are not terminal nodes. Next layer should cover stator, rotor, magnets, windings, encoder, housing, bearings, thermal design, motor control interface, manufacturing process, and cost/supply constraints.

name: Servo motor stator core
description: Stationary magnetic core of the servo motor that carries windings and helps create the rotating magnetic field for torque generation.
notes: Expansion frontier: next layer may include lamination steel, stamping/stacking, insulation, slot fill, winding layout, and thermal limits.

name: Servo motor windings
description: Copper windings that carry current to create the rotating magnetic field in the servo motor.
notes: Expansion frontier: next layer may include copper wire, insulation, winding method, impregnation, heat rise, and automated winding process constraints.

name: Permanent-magnet rotor
description: Rotor assembly using permanent magnets, usually rare-earth magnets in compact industrial servo motors, to produce high torque density and low inertia.
notes: Expansion frontier: next layer may include magnet grade, rotor shaft, magnet bonding/retention, balancing, demagnetization risk, and rotor thermal limits.

name: Servo motor encoder feedback
description: Integrated encoder or resolver feedback used to measure shaft position and speed for closed-loop servo control.
notes: Expansion frontier: next layer may include optical/magnetic/inductive encoder disk or ring, sensor IC, signal processing, mounting tolerance, cable, protocol, and calibration.

name: Servo motor bearings and shaft
description: Ball bearings and output shaft that support the rotor and transmit motor output power to the robot joint or reducer.
notes: Expansion frontier: next layer may include bearing life, preload, lubrication, shaft material, seal design, runout, vibration, and duty-cycle constraints.

name: Servo motor housing and thermal design
description: Motor frame, housing, mounting interface, protection level, and thermal path that affect size, heat rise, reliability, and integration.
notes: Expansion frontier: next layer may include die casting or machining, coatings, seals, heat dissipation, compact mounting, and washdown/environment options.

name: Servo motor cables and connectors
description: Motor power cable, encoder cable, and connectors that link the servo motor to the drive and controller.

name: Rare-earth permanent magnet material
description: Rare-earth permanent magnet material, commonly neodymium-iron-boron in compact servo motor rotors, supporting high torque density and low inertia.
notes: Expansion frontier: next layer may include NdFeB supply, magnet grade, coating, machining, thermal class, price volatility, and geopolitical supply constraints.

name: Servo motor assembly and test process
description: Assembly, encoder alignment, electrical testing, torque/speed testing, balancing, and final inspection needed to produce a reliable industrial servo motor.
notes: Expansion frontier: next layer needs better evidence for actual factory process flow, quality gates, yield, and cost drivers.

name: Servo motor feedback alignment
description: Engineering method for aligning encoder feedback with rotor position so the servo drive can commutate and control the motor accurately.
notes: Expansion frontier: needs source-backed process detail for encoder mounting, offset calibration, signal verification, and robot-joint integration.

name: Servo motor integrated brake option
description: Optional holding or safety brake integrated with a servo motor where the robot joint must hold position during power loss or emergency stop.

name: Arm links and joints
description: Mechanical arm links, joints, bearings, covers, and structural elements that define reach, stiffness, repeatability, and maintainability.
notes: Expansion frontier: next layer should cover link materials, castings/extrusions, bearing seats, joint covers, stiffness, tolerance stack-up, machining, surface treatment, and assembly constraints.

name: Robot controller and I/O
description: Robot controller, I/O, fieldbus, and integration interfaces connecting the arm to vision, conveyor, safety, and sorting decision systems.
notes: Expanded on 2026-06-07 to expose the control-stack layer a stock investor or founder would inspect: controller CPU, real-time runtime, fieldbus, safety I/O, external I/O, and diagnostics. Supplier links are candidates only and do not prove the exact BOM for the 300,000 RMB parcel cell.

name: Robot controller CPU module
description: Industrial controller CPU or embedded motion controller that runs robot-control tasks, I/O coordination, fieldbus masters, and cell-level integration logic.
notes: Investor lens: controller CPU exposure maps to PLC, PAC, and motion-control suppliers. The v0 product can use a robot OEM controller, a separate machine controller, or an integrated low-cost motion controller; this node models the purchasable control hardware layer rather than a confirmed SKU.

name: Robot real-time control runtime
description: Real-time software runtime for servo coordination, robot motion primitives, PLC logic, interpolation, watchdogs, and deterministic task scheduling.
notes: Bottleneck relevance is integration quality, not basic availability: the hard part for a parcel cell is deterministic coordination with vision, conveyor timing, safety stops, and fault recovery under low-cost hardware constraints.

name: Robot fieldbus gateway
description: Industrial network interface layer for EtherCAT, PROFINET, EtherNet/IP, Modbus TCP/RTU, OPC UA, or vendor robot-bus connections between controller, servo drives, remote I/O, safety, and WCS/PLC systems.
notes: Startup lens: this is a common source of commissioning cost and schedule risk because the physical product may be mature while exact protocol mapping, timing, and diagnostics are project-specific.

name: Robot safety I/O interface
description: Safety-rated input/output interface that carries E-stop, guard-door, light-curtain, safety scanner, enabling, and safe-stop signals between the robot controller, safety PLC, and servo STO channels.
notes: Safety I/O is commercially available, but low-cost deployments are constrained by risk assessment, validated stop behavior, wiring discipline, and restart/fault handling. This links the robot-control stack to the broader safety_system branch.

name: Robot external I/O and sensor interface
description: Digital, analog, and networked I/O that connects vacuum valves, pressure sensors, conveyor encoder pulses, photoeyes, stack lights, cabinet signals, and local maintenance controls to the robot/controller stack.
notes: Cost and reliability depend on channel count, IP rating, connectorization, spare channels, and diagnostics. For parcel sorting, this layer is where suction, conveyor, and exception-handling signals become observable to the controller.

name: Robot controller diagnostics interface
description: Diagnostic, remote-commissioning, logging, HMI, and maintenance interface for controller state, I/O faults, servo alarms, safety faults, timing errors, and recovery workflows.
notes: The hardware and vendor tools exist, but the parcel-cell value depends on app-specific fault taxonomy, recoverability, and logs that help a low-skill operator restore flow without a controls engineer on site.

name: Robot cabling and power
description: Power supplies, cabling, cable routing, connectors, and service access needed for reliable robot-arm operation in a sorting cell.

name: Robot base / mounting structure
description: Robot base, mounting frame, alignment structure, and floor or conveyor attachment needed for stable operation and installation.

name: Robot base installation and alignment process
description: Installation, leveling, anchoring, conveyor-relative alignment, vibration checking, and acceptance testing process for a low-cost robot sorting cell base.
notes: Consistency backfill: the mounting structure was less mature than its steel material child, so this node captures the missing deployment bottleneck: repeatable field alignment, anchoring, vibration control, and commissioning for a low-cost cell.

name: Robot arm assembly process
description: Assembly, calibration, wiring, joint testing, reducer installation, and final inspection processes for the robot body.

name: Conveyor integration
description: Mechanical, electrical, and controls integration with conveyor flow, induction, sensors, spacing, and downstream chutes.
notes: Bottleneck theme: low_cost_conveyor_integration. Low-cost cells are constrained by how reliably the conveyor, induction, sensing, chutes, PLC/WCS signals, and robot timing can be integrated without project-specific engineering cost.

name: Conveyor photoelectric sensors
description: Photoelectric or background-suppression sensors used to detect parcels entering, leaving, spacing, or jamming in the sorting cell.
notes: Expansion frontier: next layer may include sensor mode, mounting brackets, dust immunity, reflectivity issues, trigger timing, and maintenance.

name: Conveyor speed encoder tracking
description: Encoder or drive feedback that maps parcel detections into conveyor position so vision, robot motion, and destination timing stay synchronized.
notes: Consistency backfill: parcel detection/tracking now carries the low-jam-rate parcel-variability bottleneck, and conveyor speed/position tracking is the lower-layer timing driver. Expansion frontier: next layer may include encoder resolution, belt slip, tracking origin, PLC scan timing, and calibration against camera coordinates.

name: Parcel induction and spacing control
description: Controls logic and line setup that keep parcel spacing and presentation stable enough for scanning and robot-arm intervention.
notes: Consistency backfill: conveyor_integration is marked as a low-cost conveyor-integration bottleneck, and this lower-layer spacing/induction control method is the visible direct driver. Expansion frontier: next layer may include singulation, merge logic, gaps, parcel orientation, speed transitions, and exception handling.

name: PLC and WCS integration
description: PLC, robot controller, warehouse control system, and I/O integration that turns parcel identity into synchronized sorting actions.
notes: Expansion frontier: next layer may include fieldbus, message schema, sort plan handoff, fault recovery, logging, and commissioning workflow.

name: PLC/WCS sorting handshake and fault recovery
description: Integration method for fieldbus/I/O mapping, parcel identity handoff, sort-command timing, robot-controller acknowledgement, exception handling, logging, and restart recovery.
notes: Consistency backfill: PLC/WCS integration was less mature than its semiconductor child, so this node captures the missing software-and-controls bottleneck. Mature electronics do not prove the parcel identity, timing, acknowledgement, and exception-recovery loop.

name: Sortation chutes and bins
description: Physical outputs, chutes, bins, or lanes that receive parcels after the robot-arm sorting action.
notes: Expansion frontier: next layer may include chute geometry, jam risk, destination capacity, operator ergonomics, and parcel damage constraints.

name: Jam detection and recovery
description: Detection logic, alerts, and recovery workflow for parcels stuck in conveyor, chute, or robot-handling areas.
notes: Expansion frontier: needs field evidence for jam modes, sensor coverage, recovery time, false alarms, and operator intervention rate.

name: Sorting decision system
description: Software that maps parcel identity and destination rules to a route or output action.

name: Motion planning
description: Plans robot or actuator motion under timing, collision, parcel stability, and throughput constraints.
notes: Hard-to-develop (per ADR-0005): real-time motion planning under uncertainty (parcel pose noise, conveyor speed variation, multi-arm collision risk, and tight cycle-time targets) is a known frontier in industrial robotics. A naive planner cannot meet both throughput and reliability simultaneously.

name: Safety system
description: Guards, emergency stops, interlocks, sensors, and safety-rated controls suitable for warehouse operation.

name: Mechanical structure
description: Frame, mounts, actuated elements, bins, chutes, cable routing, and service access structure.

name: Maintenance workflow
description: Inspection, jam clearing, spare parts, cleaning, calibration, and operator escalation workflow.
notes: Bottleneck theme: maintenance_cost_control. Maintenance workflow limits adoption when jams, cleaning, suction-cup wear, calibration drift, spare parts, and operator escalation consume the labor savings from automation.

name: Cost-optimized hardware stack
description: Hardware selection and integration that keeps cameras, compute, actuators, controls, frame, safety, and install cost inside the 300,000 RMB target.

name: Delta robot sorter candidate
description: Use a high-speed delta robot for lightweight parcels where reach, payload, and object variability fit the mechanism.
notes: Adjacent product candidate only. It is not an internal route of low_cost_parcel_sorting_robot_300k_rmb unless the product boundary is explicitly changed.

name: Delta robot parcel-variability jam control
description: Delta-robot-specific method for limiting jams and missed picks under variable parcel size, packaging deformation, conveyor spacing, and high-speed pick-window constraints.
notes: Consistency backfill: delta_robot_sorting carried the low-jam-rate bottleneck, but its direct children were generic shared modules. This node captures the missing delta-specific parcel-variability and jam-control driver.

name: Conveyor diverter sorter candidate
description: Use lower-cost conveyor diverters, pushers, belts, or actuated guides instead of robotic picking.
notes: Adjacent product candidate only. It is not an internal route of low_cost_parcel_sorting_robot_300k_rmb unless the product boundary is explicitly changed.

name: Mobile robot sorter candidate
description: Use mobile robots to carry parcels or bins between induction and destinations.
notes: Adjacent product candidate only. It is not an internal route of low_cost_parcel_sorting_robot_300k_rmb unless the product boundary is explicitly changed.

name: Hybrid human-robot assisted sorter candidate
description: Use automation for recognition, routing, and assistive motion while humans handle difficult parcels or exceptions.
notes: Adjacent product candidate only. It is not an internal route of low_cost_parcel_sorting_robot_300k_rmb unless the product boundary is explicitly changed.

name: Total system cost
description: Full deployed cost of the sorting cell, including hardware, integration, and installation.

name: Parcels per hour
description: Sustained parcel throughput under realistic parcel mix and exception rates.

metrics.name: Throughput
metrics.description: Unreviewed p50 benchmark for one robotic suction/vision parcel induction or sorting station. Vendor-adjacent sources range from 325-400 parcels/hour for lower-throughput robot sort cells to 1,500-1,800 parcels/hour for robotic induction/singulation modules.

notes: Performance benchmark is vendor-adjacent and should not be read as a reviewed sustained field throughput. The current v0 product likely bottlenecks at induction spacing, vision/tracking, suction grasp success, robot cycle time, and downstream WCS/conveyor synchronization before it can use larger sorter capacity.

name: Sorting accuracy
description: Share of parcels routed to the correct output without human correction.

metrics.name: Accuracy
metrics.description: Vendor-adjacent benchmark combining singulation accuracy, picking accuracy, barcode read rate, and correct-output sort accuracy. It is not yet reviewed field sort accuracy for the v0 cell.

notes: The metric blends adjacent vendor claims because public pages usually report picking, singulation, barcode, or correct-output accuracy separately. Human review should split these if field data becomes available.

name: Allowed parcel weight range
description: Supported parcel weight envelope for reliable sorting.

metrics.name: Weight range
metrics.currentValue: 0.003-35 kg adjacent benchmark envelope; v0 target remains 0.05-25 kg mixed parcels
metrics.description: Adjacent robot parcel-handling pages span very light mailers up to 35 kg, but the v0 suction-cell target keeps a narrower 0.05-25 kg envelope.

notes: Weight envelope is not reviewed for this exact 300,000 RMB cell. Suction cup geometry, payload, acceleration limits, and parcel packaging material will narrow the usable field range.

name: Allowed parcel size range
description: Supported parcel dimensions and shape variability.

metrics.name: Size range
metrics.currentValue: 76 x 76 x 2.5 mm to 700 x 700 x 1200 mm adjacent benchmark envelope; v0 target longest dimension up to 700 mm
metrics.description: Adjacent benchmark envelope from robot parcel sort/singulation sources. The v0 product target remains narrower and should be validated against suction reach, camera field-of-view, and conveyor spacing.

notes: Size envelope is an adjacent benchmark, not reviewed field evidence for the active product. Irregular polybags and soft packs may be more limiting than nominal box dimensions.

name: Failure / jam rate
description: Rate of jams, failed picks, failed diverts, or stoppages.

metrics.name: Jam rate
metrics.description: Proxy benchmark from adjacent vendor claims: double-parcel grasp, failed grasp, unread barcode diversion, and uptime. This is not yet a direct reviewed jam/stoppage rate.

notes: The current range should be interpreted as exception-risk order of magnitude. Real jam rate needs field logs that distinguish failed pick, double pick, barcode no-read, conveyor jam, chute jam, and stop/recovery events.

name: Human intervention rate
description: Share of parcels or operating time requiring manual intervention.

metrics.name: Intervention rate
metrics.description: Proxy benchmark for manual exception handling, based on adjacent pick accuracy, barcode no-read diversion, in-size sortability, and uptime claims.

notes: Manual intervention remains one of the weakest public-data areas. Human review should replace this proxy with shift-level exception logs from a real deployment.

name: Installation time
description: Time required to install and commission one sorting cell.

metrics.name: Install time
metrics.description: Adjacent deployment benchmark for a pre-engineered robotic parcel station, not a guaranteed installation duration for every conveyor/WCS site.

notes: Install time depends heavily on brownfield conveyor geometry, guarding, WCS integration, compressed air, electrical work, and acceptance testing.

name: Maintenance cost
description: Ongoing maintenance cost including labor, spares, downtime, and recalibration.

metrics.name: Maintenance cost
metrics.description: Low-confidence proxy derived from 4-15% annual maintenance rules for industrial robots and adjacent equipment applied to the 300,000 RMB replacement value; p50 uses roughly 8%.

notes: Unreviewed annual run-rate estimate for the 300,000 RMB parcel sorting cell. Includes preventive robot PM, suction-cup and EOAT wear, conveyor and sensor maintenance, calibration, and internal or contractor labor. Excludes downtime opportunity cost, major overhauls, and WCS subscription/support unless separately quoted. Replace with site maintenance logs, integrator quotes, and spare-part consumption data when available.

name: Payback period
description: Time needed for labor savings or throughput value to recover deployed cost.

metrics.name: Payback
metrics.description: Generic parcel-sortation automation ROI benchmark. Treat as a conservative reference point; the 300,000 RMB robotic cell needs a site-specific labor, volume, uptime, and maintenance model.

notes: FloStor's ROI benchmark is for broader parcel sortation automation and often higher-CAPEX systems. The v0 product may pay back faster or slower depending on wage level, parcel volume, shift count, exception rate, and maintenance cost.

name: Real-time machine vision
description: Computer vision and sensing principles that support parcel localization and label recognition.
notes: Frontier candidate: next layer should distinguish detection backbones (classical CV vs CNN-based vs transformer-based), label/text reading approaches, and real-time inference constraints relevant to parcel-sorting throughput targets.

name: Queuing and flow variability
description: Parcel arrival variability, spacing, and exception distribution determine whether throughput targets are realistic.
notes: Frontier candidate: next layer should model induction strategies, arrival distributions (Poisson vs burst), exception-rate distributions, and how upstream depalletization variability propagates into the sorter.

name: Modular cell manufacturing
description: Build the sorting cell from repeatable modules that can be assembled, installed, serviced, and costed predictably.
notes: Frontier candidate: next layer should model station-by-station fab steps, jig/fixture standardization, line-side parts-supply, integration test protocols, and per-module cost roll-up.

name: Warehouse machine safety standard
description: Local machine safety, guarding, emergency-stop, and operator protection requirements for warehouse automation.

name: Refined copper conductor material
description: Refined copper used in motor windings, power cabling, PCBs, connectors, servo drives, sensors, and control cabinets.

name: Copper ore mining and refining chain
description: Mining, concentrating, smelting, refining, and recycling chain that supplies refined copper for robot electrical systems.
notes: Mineral-level frontier: next layer may model ore grade, mine permitting, smelting/refining capacity, recycled copper, sulfuric acid constraints, and regional supply risk.

name: Electrical steel lamination material
description: Electrical steel sheet used in servo motor stator laminations to carry magnetic flux with controlled losses.
notes: Material frontier: next layer may include silicon steel grade, rolling, annealing, coating, stamping, stack bonding, and loss testing.

name: Alloy steel precision material
description: Alloy steel used in reducer splines, shafts, bearings, gears, arm joints, and load-bearing robot structures.
notes: Material frontier: next layer may include steel grade, heat treatment, cleanliness, forging/casting/rolling route, machining stock, and bearing steel requirements.

name: Iron ore and steelmaking chain
description: Iron ore mining, steelmaking, alloying, recycling, and rolling chain that supplies structural and precision steels for the robot.
notes: Mineral-level frontier: next layer may model iron ore, scrap supply, alloying elements, blast furnace/basic oxygen furnace route, electric-arc furnace route, energy intensity, and emissions.

name: Bauxite, alumina, and aluminum chain
description: Bauxite mining, alumina refining, aluminum smelting, recycling, extrusion, casting, and machining chain for lightweight robot and conveyor structures.
notes: Mineral-level frontier: next layer may model bauxite ore, Bayer alumina refining, Hall-Heroult smelting, recycled aluminum, energy cost, and extrusion/casting capacity.

name: Aluminum structural material
description: Aluminum castings, extrusions, plates, and machined parts used where low mass, corrosion resistance, or easy assembly matters.
notes: Material frontier: next layer may include alloy series, extrusion die, casting route, CNC machining, surface treatment, and recycling.

name: Quartz, silica, and silicon chain
description: Quartz or quartzite mining, silicon metal production, and high-purity silicon processing chain used for semiconductors, sensors, and some industrial materials.
notes: Mineral-level frontier: next layer may model quartz quality, submerged-arc furnace silicon metal, polysilicon, wafer fabrication, chip packaging, and supply concentration.

name: Semiconductor-grade silicon and electronics
description: High-purity silicon and electronics supply chain used in image sensors, processors, power semiconductors, encoders, PLCs, and servo-drive control electronics.
notes: Material frontier: next layer may include wafer fab, power device process, image sensor process, IC packaging, PCB assembly, and export-control or capacity constraints.

name: NdPr rare-earth feedstock
description: Neodymium-praseodymium rare-earth feedstock used in high-strength permanent magnets for compact servo motors.
notes: Mineral-level frontier: next layer may include bastnaesite/monazite mining, separation, oxide-to-metal conversion, magnet alloying, and regional supply concentration.

name: Dysprosium / terbium heavy rare-earth additives
description: Heavy rare-earth additives used where NdFeB magnets need higher temperature performance or coercivity.
notes: Mineral-level frontier: next layer may include heavy-rare-earth ore sources, separation capacity, diffusion process, substitution, recycling, and price volatility.

name: Boron and iron magnet matrix material
description: Iron and boron-containing matrix material used with neodymium/praseodymium in NdFeB permanent magnets.
notes: Material frontier: next layer may include ferroboron/borates, iron powder or alloy feedstock, powder metallurgy, sintering, coating, and magnet recycling.

name: Petrochemical elastomer feedstock
description: Polymer and elastomer feedstock used for suction cups, seals, hoses, cable jackets, and protective covers.
notes: Raw-material frontier: next layer may include silicone, nitrile, polyurethane, rubber compounding, wear additives, molding, petrochemical feedstock, and recycling/disposal.

name: Affordable small warehouse automation
description: Lower-cost automation for warehouses that cannot justify large centralized sortation systems.

targetContext.facilitySize: 1,000–5,000 m² floor area, 1–2 sorting cells, single shift to two shifts depending on volume
targetContext.dailyThroughput: Up to ~30,000 parcels/day per cell at sustained operation; typical small-warehouse demand 5,000–20,000 parcels/day
targetContext.parcelSpecRange: Cuboid + soft pack mixed flow, 0.05–25 kg, longest dimension up to 700 mm; weight/size envelopes per existing allowed_parcel_weight/size_range metrics
targetContext.environment: Indoor logistics warehouse in 2025-China context, ambient temperature 5–35 °C, dust acceptable, no explosion-proofing required
targetContext.shiftPattern: Single + extended evening shift typical; 24/7 not assumed at this price point

name: 300,000 RMB parcel-sorting robot (gripper variant)
description: Deferred-expansion sibling Product candidate to low_cost_parcel_sorting_robot_300k_rmb. Same Capability target (affordable_small_warehouse_automation), but uses a mechanical gripper end-effector instead of vacuum suction. Not expanded in v0; preserved here so its substantive sub-tree from the retired industrial_robot_arm_gripper_route has a home.
notes: Created per ADR-0004 step 5 (route retirement). Stays out of active graph scope: there is no inbound edge from any node reachable from low_cost_parcel_sorting_robot_300k_rmb, only outbound edges from this Product to shared modules and to the Capability.

name: Mechanical gripper end-effector module
description: Deferred placeholder module for the gripper sibling Product. It represents a mechanical finger or clamp end-effector branch and is intentionally not expanded inside the active vacuum-suction v0 product.
notes: Created to keep the gripper sibling Product boundary separate from the active suction product. Expand only after the user clarifies the gripper architecture, target parcels, contact mechanics, cost target, and whether hybrid gripper+suction variants should remain separate.

name: Industrial robot arm body cost
description: Installed-component cost contribution of the bare 6-axis robot arm body (joints, links, reducers, servo motors, controller interfaces) to the v0 parcel-sorting cell. Mid-tier 2025-China industrial pricing for arms in the 5-10 kg payload, sub-1 m reach class.
notes: Rough 2025-China industrial estimate recalibrated on 2026-06-07 from public 6/7 kg six-axis robot price listings and a payload/reach price guide. Very low marketplace listings exist below this band, but this node is intended to represent a mid-tier purchasable industrial arm body/control bundle rather than the cheapest quoted manipulator. Marked unreviewed for human verification per ADR-0001.

name: Precision reducer gearbox cost
description: Allocated cost contribution of robot joint precision reducers inside the bare robot arm body bundle.
notes: Consistency backfill: the robot-arm bundle is a high-cost subsystem in the graph, but none of its direct children originally carried cost. This allocates the largest expected cost driver to precision reducers so cost-mode colour has an explanatory child source; keep unreviewed until replaced with supplier or teardown evidence.

name: Reducer lubrication and life testing cost
description: Allocated cost contribution of reducer endurance testing, lubrication qualification, backlash verification, and acceptance testing inside the precision-reducer cost.
notes: Consistency backfill: precision-reducer cost should be explained by an immature lower-layer cost driver. This allocates the high-cost reducer bottleneck to life-test and qualification capability rather than raw alloy steel.

name: Industrial servo motor cost
description: Allocated cost contribution of servo motors inside the bare robot arm body bundle.
notes: Consistency backfill allocation from the robot-arm bundle estimate; unreviewed until replaced with supplier or teardown evidence.

name: Servo drive controller cost
description: Allocated cost contribution of servo-drive electronics and control hardware inside the bare robot arm body bundle.
notes: Consistency backfill allocation from the robot-arm bundle estimate; unreviewed until replaced with supplier or teardown evidence.

name: Arm links and joints cost
description: Allocated cost contribution of robot arm links, joint housings, and mechanical joint hardware inside the bare robot arm body bundle.
notes: Consistency backfill allocation from the robot-arm bundle estimate; unreviewed until replaced with supplier or teardown evidence.

name: Robot controller I/O cost
description: Allocated cost contribution of robot controller I/O boards and interface hardware inside the bare robot arm body bundle.
notes: Consistency backfill allocation from the robot-arm bundle estimate; unreviewed until replaced with supplier or teardown evidence.

name: Robot controller CPU module cost
description: Allocated cost contribution of the controller CPU or embedded motion-controller hardware inside the robot controller and I/O bundle.
notes: Controller/I-O child allocation backfill. This is not a supplier quote; it keeps the recursive cost model explicit until a BOM, controller SKU, or teardown replaces it.

name: Robot real-time control runtime cost
description: Allocated cost contribution of bundled runtime, motion-control libraries, and controller firmware configuration inside the robot controller and I/O bundle.
notes: Controller/I/O child allocation backfill. Low-cost robot controllers often bundle the runtime with hardware, so this is a small allocated cost placeholder rather than a separately quoted software license.

name: Robot fieldbus gateway cost
description: Allocated cost contribution of fieldbus, industrial Ethernet, and gateway interface hardware inside the robot controller and I/O bundle.
notes: Controller/I/O child allocation backfill. Actual cost depends on whether EtherCAT, PROFINET, EtherNet/IP, Modbus, or vendor robot-bus interfaces are native or require add-on modules.

name: Robot safety I/O interface cost
description: Allocated cost contribution of safety-rated I/O channels, safe-stop interfaces, and E-stop/guard integration inside the robot controller and I/O bundle.
notes: Controller/I/O child allocation backfill. It captures the controller-side safety interface only; the broader cell safety system remains costed separately.

name: Robot external I/O and sensor interface cost
description: Allocated cost contribution of digital, analog, and networked I/O channels that connect valves, sensors, encoders, photoeyes, and cabinet signals to the robot controller.
notes: Controller/I/O child allocation backfill. Replace with an explicit channel-count BOM once the parcel-cell wiring and sensor map are reviewed.

name: Robot controller diagnostics interface cost
description: Allocated cost contribution of bundled diagnostics, logging, remote commissioning hooks, and controller maintenance interface inside the robot controller and I/O bundle.
notes: Controller/I/O child allocation backfill. Most value here is integration and recoverability work; this metric is only the controller-bundle allocation, not full field commissioning labor.

name: Robot cabling and power cost
description: Allocated cost contribution of robot cabling, connectors, and internal power distribution inside the bare robot arm body bundle.
notes: Consistency backfill allocation from the robot-arm bundle estimate; unreviewed until replaced with supplier or teardown evidence.

name: Robot base mounting structure cost
description: Allocated cost contribution of the robot base and mounting structure inside the bare robot arm body bundle.
notes: Consistency backfill allocation from the robot-arm bundle estimate; unreviewed until replaced with supplier or teardown evidence.

name: End effector module cost
description: Installed-component cost contribution of the vacuum suction end-of-arm tooling module (cup array, ejector or pump, valves, pressure sensing) to the v0 parcel-sorting cell.
notes: Rough 2025-China industrial estimate. Pricing the end-effector as a bundled module intercepts recursion through cup-array / ejector / valves / pressure-sensing leaves. Marked unreviewed for human verification.

name: Parcel manipulation subsystem integration cost
description: Integration-only cost premium for the manipulation subsystem (cabling, brackets, sequencing/calibration) above the per-component cost of arm body, end-effector, and motion planning that the rollup walker counts via the product-level requires edges.
notes: Integration cost premium for the manipulation module — wiring, calibration, fixturing on top of the bare arm + end-effector + planning subsystems. Marked unreviewed for human verification.

name: Industrial area-scan camera cost
description: Installed-component cost contribution of an industrial global-shutter area-scan camera (mid-resolution, GigE/USB3) plus IO and mounting, in the v0 parcel-sorting cell.
notes: Rough 2025-China industrial estimate. Reflects Hikrobot / Daheng / Basler-equivalent ranges suitable for parcel-label imaging at conveyor speed. Marked unreviewed for human verification.

name: Machine vision lens and optics cost
description: Installed-component cost contribution of the C-mount industrial lens and optics needed to focus parcel labels onto the camera sensor.
notes: Rough 2025 estimate covering standard fixed-focal-length C-mount lenses. High-end metrology lenses can be much more expensive; this range is utility imaging only. Marked unreviewed for human verification.

name: Controlled machine-vision lighting cost
description: Installed-component cost contribution of an industrial LED lighting fixture (bar / ring / dome) plus controller, sized for parcel-label illumination on one cell.
notes: Rough 2025-China estimate per fixture. Multi-fixture deployments and strobed controllers can push higher. Marked unreviewed for human verification.

name: Vision processing compute cost
description: Installed-component cost contribution of a fanless industrial PC with mid-tier GPU/accelerator, suitable for real-time barcode/OCR plus light detection inference at conveyor speed.
notes: Rough 2025-China estimate. Smart-camera embedded options sit at the lower end; high-end perception stacks land well above this range. Marked unreviewed for human verification.

name: Conveyor integration hardware cost
description: Installed-component cost contribution of the conveyor section, photoelectric sensors, speed encoder, PLC, and chutes/lanes hardware integrated into one sorting cell.
notes: Rough 2025-China estimate scoped to a single small sorting cell. Conveyor cost scales strongly with length, lane count, and chute geometry. Marked unreviewed for human verification.

name: PLC and WCS integration cost
description: Allocated cost contribution of PLC hardware, WCS interface work, commissioning, and control cabinet integration inside the conveyor-integration bundle.
notes: Consistency backfill: the 55,000 RMB conveyor-integration bundle was high-cost in the graph, but none of its direct children carried cost. This allocates the largest expected cost driver to PLC/WCS integration so cost-mode colour has an explanatory child source.

name: PLC/WCS sorting handshake and fault recovery cost
description: Allocated cost contribution of PLC/WCS handshake implementation, exception handling, commissioning, logging, and restart-recovery work inside the PLC/WCS integration cost.
notes: Consistency backfill: PLC/WCS integration was high-cost, but the cost driver was not visible one layer down. This allocates the high-cost portion to handshake/fault-recovery integration work rather than semiconductor availability.

name: Sortation chutes and bins cost
description: Allocated cost contribution of chutes, bins, guide plates, and lane hardware inside the conveyor-integration bundle.
notes: Consistency backfill allocation from the conveyor-integration bundle estimate; unreviewed until replaced with supplier or teardown evidence.

name: Conveyor speed encoder tracking cost
description: Allocated cost contribution of speed encoder hardware, mounts, wiring, and tracking integration inside the conveyor-integration bundle.
notes: Consistency backfill allocation from the conveyor-integration bundle estimate; unreviewed until replaced with supplier or teardown evidence.

name: Conveyor photoelectric sensors cost

name: Safety system cost
description: Installed-component cost contribution of perimeter guarding, light curtains, e-stop circuitry, safety relays/PLC, and interlocked-door hardware for one cell.
notes: Rough 2025-China estimate. Safety scope varies by site standard and risk-assessment outcome. Marked unreviewed for human verification.

name: Mechanical structure cost
description: Installed-component cost contribution of the cell frame, robot pedestal, electrical cabinet enclosure, cable trays, and structural sheet-metal/extrusion parts outside the conveyor and arm proper.
notes: Rough 2025-China estimate. Custom mechanical work (specialty frame, tooling) can push cost higher. Marked unreviewed for human verification.

name: Sorting decision system cost
description: Allocated cost contribution of the sorting decision software (rule engine, destination mapping, WCS interface, basic dashboard) per cell.
notes: Rough 2025 estimate per cell. Either a vendor license fee or an internal-build allocation amortized to one cell. Marked unreviewed for human verification.

name: Motion planning software cost
description: Allocated cost contribution of motion-planning software per cell — slice of an in-house planner or vendor pick-and-place library, amortized to a single sorting cell.
notes: Rough 2025 amortized per-cell estimate. R&D for novel planners is not captured here. Marked unreviewed for human verification.

name: Parcel detection and tracking cost
description: Allocated cost contribution of parcel detection-and-tracking software components (detection model integration, parcel pose tracker, conveyor-coordinate pipeline) per cell. Compute hardware is separately costed under vision_processing_compute.
notes: Rough 2025 allocated estimate per cell. Proprietary model training and labelling cost not allocated here. Marked unreviewed for human verification.

name: Barcode / OCR reading software cost
description: Allocated per-cell cost for barcode/OCR software integration, decoder/OCR runtime licensing, no-read handling, and benchmark setup. Reader hardware and compute are costed separately.
notes: Rough 2025 per-cell allocation. The figure is scoped to software/integration only, excluding camera, lighting, compute, and full WCS license costs.

name: Parcel label localization cost
description: Allocated per-cell cost for label-region localization tuning, configuration, and validation.
notes: Small software-allocation placeholder; replace with vendor quote or internal engineering amortization once reviewed.

name: Industrial barcode decoding runtime cost
description: Allocated per-cell cost for barcode decoder runtime licensing or bundled configuration inside the parcel identification pipeline.
notes: Placeholder allocation only. Some vendors bundle decoding with reader hardware; this node keeps the software dependency visible without asserting separate line-item pricing.

name: Parcel OCR model runtime cost
description: Allocated per-cell cost for OCR model runtime configuration and validation for parcel label text fallback.
notes: Placeholder allocation for OCR runtime and tuning. Training data and benchmark work are represented by separate child metrics.

name: Barcode / OCR no-read recovery cost
description: Allocated per-cell cost for no-read retry logic, confidence thresholds, diagnostics, WCS exception handoff, and manual-keying workflow integration.
notes: Placeholder allocation for exception handling. The operational cost of manual exception labor is not included here.

name: Parcel label training dataset cost
description: Allocated per-cell amortized cost for parcel-label data collection, annotation, and dataset maintenance used by localization/OCR/no-read analysis.
notes: Very rough amortized allocation. This excludes any large one-off data program and should be replaced with project-specific labeling economics.

name: Barcode / OCR benchmark protocol cost
description: Allocated per-cell cost for defining and running barcode/OCR benchmark checks such as read rate, false read rate, latency, and exception rate.
notes: Small placeholder allocation for benchmark design and repeatable acceptance checks, not ongoing production QA labor.

name: Maintenance workflow first-year spares and tooling cost
description: Cost contribution of the initial spares kit, basic maintenance tooling, and operator training materials shipped with one cell. Recurring annual maintenance is tracked separately under the maintenance_cost metric.
notes: Rough 2025-China estimate for initial spares plus operator tooling. Annual recurring maintenance lives on the maintenance_cost metric. Marked unreviewed for human verification.
